title: Episode 17: Accessibility Agents
description: 55 agents across 3 teams and 5 platforms, 54+ slash commands, custom agents, and agentic accessibility workflows.
concepts: What accessibility agents are: specialized AI assistants for a11y tasks
How agents extend GitHub Copilot with domain expertise
The full ecosystem: 55 agents, 3 teams, 5 platforms
Team 1 - Accessibility (26 agents): web, document, mobile auditing
Team 2 - GitHub Workflow (12 agents): issues, PRs, analytics, templates
Team 3 - Developer Tools (6 agents): Python, desktop, custom tools
Slash commands: 54+ commands organized by workflow
High-impact starting points: which agents and commands to try first
Slash commands that save time: /my-issues, /review-pr, /triage, /daily-briefing, /a11y-update
Orchestrator agents: @nexus, @accessibility-lead, @web-accessibility-wizard
How the three teams connect in multi-agent workflows
How to invoke an agent in Copilot Chat
Installing and configuring agents from .github config files
Agent instruction files and how they customize behavior
Building your own custom agent with agent.md files
Agentic workflows: chaining multiple agents together
How agents amplify skills: the manual skill first, then the agent
Real-world examples of agent-assisted contributions
Limitations: agents suggest, humans decide and verify
Go deeper: Appendix V has all 54+ commands, Episode 39 walks through every agent
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're exploring accessibility agents: what they are, where they run, how to decide whether you're actually ready to use one, and how to contribute to an open ecosystem of agents without treating automation like magic.

[JAMIE]
And I'm glad we're starting there, because a lot of learners hear "AI agents" and think, great, now the tool will just do accessibility for me.

[ALEX]
Right, and this chapter pushes back on that. The core idea is simple: skill first, agent second. An agent multiplies a skill you already have. It does not create that skill for you.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
A quick orientation note before we go deeper. There's an audio companion for this material, related appendices for agents and Copilot reference material, and a set of authoritative sources from GitHub Docs and VS Code Docs. If you want the official product behavior, those docs are the source of truth.

[JAMIE]
So this lesson is teaching practice and workflow, but not replacing the official documentation.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an important product note: newer VS Code versions include an Agents window in stable as a preview feature. That does not replace custom accessibility agents. It gives you a dedicated place to run and organize agent sessions, review changed files, and manage work across projects.

[JAMIE]
So learners should think, custom agents are still the substance, and the Agents window is one interface for working with them.

[ALEX]
Perfectly said.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's frame the landscape. The repository highlighted in this chapter is a growing open source ecosystem of AI-powered agents organized into three teams and deployable across five platforms.

[JAMIE]
I noticed one number early on says fifty-five agents, and another later says eighty. How should learners hear that?

[ALEX]
As a living project. The exact count can change as the ecosystem grows. The important ideas are the structure and the breadth: three teams, multiple platforms, and a wide range of workflows. You are not expected to use every agent. You're expected to find the agents that match skills you already built manually.

[JAMIE]
And the platforms matter too, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. These agents aren't trapped in one editor. The chapter positions them across GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Claude Desktop, and Codex CLI. So the lesson isn't "use this one exact interface." It's "understand the pattern, then choose the platform that fits your workflow and access needs."

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before anyone starts, what's the checklist?

[ALEX]
There's a real prerequisites checklist, and it matters. First, learners should already have workshop setup completed: Git, VS Code, and a GitHub account. Second, GitHub Copilot should already be enabled and working in VS Code. Third, Copilot access is required, but the free tier is enough for this workshop. Fourth, your repository should include a .github slash agents folder, or you should be prepared to create custom agents.

[JAMIE]
And then there's the deeper prerequisite: not just software, but skill.

[ALEX]
Yes. The chapter explicitly maps agent categories to manual experience. For GitHub workflow agents like daily briefings, issue tracking, pull request review, and analytics, you should already know how to navigate repositories, file issues, review pull requests, and explore repository insights.

[JAMIE]
So if I've never reviewed a pull request by hand, I should not ask an agent to review one and assume I understand the result.

[ALEX]
Correct. For accessibility monitoring agents, you should already know how to file an accessibility bug, apply accessibility labels, and inspect things like heading hierarchy. For template creation agents, you should already have designed and tested templates manually. For web accessibility auditing agents, you should already understand WCAG success criteria and have tested pages with assistive technology.

[JAMIE]
And the document-specific agents have their own manual prerequisites too.

[ALEX]
They do. If you want help with Word, Excel, PDF, or EPUB accessibility, you should already know something about document structure and manual accessibility review. If you want remediation agents, you should understand tagging, alternative text, bookmarks, or the relevant toolchain. Python or wxPython agents assume Python knowledge and GUI accessibility basics. Developer tool agents assume CI or testing experience.

[JAMIE]
So the self-check question is: could I do this manually right now?

[ALEX]
Exactly. If the answer is no, learn the manual skill first.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
This chapter also includes a workshop recommendation and a challenge set, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. This is an exploration and validation chapter. The challenge sequence asks learners to discover agents, validate one against their own manual understanding, inspect an agent's instructions, and optionally improve an existing agent or propose a new one.

[JAMIE]
Let's walk that in plain language.

[ALEX]
Challenge 15.1 is agent discovery mapping. The goal is to identify three to five agents that match skills you already have from earlier workshop work. The recommended starting set, especially if the ecosystem feels large, is daily briefing, issue tracker, and pull request review.

[JAMIE]
And the workflow is practical.

[ALEX]
Very practical. Fork the accessibility-agents repository on GitHub. Open the repository. Review the list of agents. For each one, ask yourself whether you've performed that task manually. Then post a comment on your assigned challenge issue that maps each chosen agent to the manual skill that makes you ready.

[JAMIE]
So not just "I want to use this," but "I am ready because I already did this work myself."

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[JAMIE]
Then comes validation.

[ALEX]
Challenge 15.2 asks you to clone your fork into VS Code or open it in github.dev, open Copilot Chat, choose one agent from your discovery list, run a simple prompt, and then evaluate the output against your manual expectations.

[JAMIE]
That evaluation step feels important.

[ALEX]
It's essential. The automation check for this chapter is explicitly none. Agent output always requires human judgment. You're expected to read the output carefully and say whether it looks accurate, helpful, incomplete, or questionable.

[JAMIE]
And Challenge 15.3 goes inside the agent itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. Agent instructions deep dive. You read one agent source file and assess what it can and cannot do. That helps learners move from "AI said a thing" to "I understand how this tool is framed, constrained, and prompted."

[JAMIE]
Then there are optional hackathon-style extensions.

[ALEX]
Right. Improve an existing agent by finding a gap in its instructions and opening a pull request, or propose a new agent for a workflow the ecosystem doesn't yet cover.

[JAMIE]
And when learners finish?

[ALEX]
They submit evidence. The expected evidence is usually an issue comment showing agent output and your evaluation. The expected outcomes are that you can match agents to your current skills, test them critically, inspect their instructions, and begin thinking like a contributor rather than just a user.

[JAMIE]
What if someone gets stuck?

[ALEX]
The chapter explicitly normalizes that. If you get stuck, narrow the scope. Start with the simplest agents. Use one short prompt. Compare results to something you already know how to do manually. The learning moment is not "the agent was perfect." The learning moment is "I can judge what the agent did."

[JAMIE]
And there's even a teaching pattern behind this.

[ALEX]
Yes: explore, validate, read internals, optionally contribute. That's the learning pattern of the chapter.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There's also a capstone note that sounds unusually direct.

[ALEX]
It does, and we should keep it. One of the most important tasks in the chapter is to share workshop feedback. Not busywork"”feedback that helps improve the curriculum, tooling, and accessibility of the learning experience.

[JAMIE]
So submitting workshop feedback is framed as a genuine contribution.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
I saw a table of contents in the source, but for listeners, maybe we should turn that into a road map.

[ALEX]
Good idea. Here's the road map in plain speech: first, the guiding principle of skill first, agent second. Then setup and configuration. Then the ecosystem and team structure. Then multi-platform deployment beyond VS Code. Then detailed hands-on reference for specific agents. Then slash commands and prompts. Then contributing your own agents or improving existing ones. Then the bigger orchestration picture. Then GitHub Desktop, GitHub CLI, and Copilot CLI. And finally, accessibility shortcuts, troubleshooting, and the official source trail.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's come back to the principle, because it is the foundation for everything else. Every agent has a manual prerequisite. If you have not done the corresponding skill by hand, the agent is not ready for you yet, and you are not ready for it.

[JAMIE]
That sounds strict, but honestly, it's protective.

[ALEX]
Very much so. Without that rule, agents create false confidence. A learner might get a polished summary of issues without understanding labels, timelines, duplicate reports, or severity. Or get a PR review without understanding diffs, testing, or risk.

[JAMIE]
So the "learning cards" for this principle would be things like: automation amplifies skill, manual fluency comes first, and trust requires verification.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Those are the takeaways.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now setup. If someone wants to begin using these agents, what does that look like?

[ALEX]
The chapter includes a quick install path with platform-specific one-command setup for macOS or Linux and for Windows PowerShell. The exact commands belong in the written material because they can change, but the idea is that the repository is designed to be installed and explored quickly.

[JAMIE]
So in audio, we emphasize the workflow, not recite volatile commands.

[ALEX]
Right. Then comes workshop setup: fork the repository, clone your fork locally, and open it in VS Code or another supported environment.

[JAMIE]
And there's a prerequisites section inside setup too.

[ALEX]
Yes. It reinforces the need for Git, GitHub, VS Code, and Copilot readiness. Then there's a key concept: how agents are discovered.

[JAMIE]
Meaning how the platform even knows an agent exists.

[ALEX]
Correct. Agents typically travel with the repository through convention-based files and folders, especially under .github. That means repository context matters. If the repo includes agent definitions, compatible tools can detect and expose them.

[JAMIE]
That "travel with your repo" idea is powerful. It means the workflow can move with forks and collaborators.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And there's also an optional personalization step. You can customize preferences like your GitHub username, the repositories you work on most, your preferred output format, and notification priority.

[JAMIE]
So this chapter even includes a personal preferences section.

[ALEX]
It does. In effect, it models the kinds of settings that make agent output more useful and more accessible to you. Maybe you want concise bullet points. Maybe you prefer structured sections. Maybe you want urgent notifications first. Those preferences shape the interaction.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's talk about invoking agents on GitHub dot com, because not everyone wants to live in the editor.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. There are two main web-based paths highlighted. One is Copilot Chat with task mode. The other is assigning an issue to Copilot.

[JAMIE]
So learners can interact in the browser, not just locally.

[ALEX]
Yes, and the chapter also points out browser-native Copilot features on GitHub itself: pull request summaries, pull request review help, Copilot in issues, GitHub Models as a free AI playground, and Copilot-drafted release notes.

[JAMIE]
That sounds broader than "custom agents."

[ALEX]
It is. The lesson is partly about custom agents and partly about the surrounding AI ecosystem on GitHub. The learning cards for this section would emphasize setup, discovery, repo-scoped behavior, and browser-native options.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now the ecosystem section. We mentioned three teams earlier. Let's unpack them.

[ALEX]
Team one is Accessibility, the largest cluster. These agents focus on accessibility workflows: auditing, checking, remediating, and tracking accessibility concerns across web, documents, and code-adjacent tasks.

[JAMIE]
Team two is GitHub Workflow.

[ALEX]
Right. Those agents support issue triage, PR review, daily status awareness, analytics, and workflow management around collaboration.

[JAMIE]
And team three is Developer Tools.

[ALEX]
Yes. That group covers more technical workflows like CI accessibility checks, test automation, and tool-assisted development patterns.

[JAMIE]
Then there's a supporting ecosystem beyond the agents themselves.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The chapter highlights that the ecosystem includes not only agent files but prompts, slash commands, cloud features, hooks, platform integrations, and contribution pathways. For example, hook-based enforcement in tools like Claude Code can apply checks or automation rules at the right moment in a development workflow.

[JAMIE]
So an agent isn't always a chat personality. Sometimes it's part of a workflow system.

[ALEX]
Well said. The chapter also asks a design question: what would you build? That opens the contribution paths.

[JAMIE]
And those paths include improving an existing agent, proposing a new one, adding new workflows, and helping shape the roadmap.

[ALEX]
Yes. The roadmap section reminds learners this is evolving. You're not studying a finished museum exhibit. You're entering a live open source ecosystem.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Then we go beyond VS Code entirely.

[ALEX]
Right. Multi-platform deployment is a major idea here. The same general agent concepts can work across five platforms, but each platform has different strengths.

[JAMIE]
Let's do the "when to use each" version.

[ALEX]
GitHub Copilot is recommended for most learners because it integrates well with common GitHub and VS Code workflows. Claude Code is positioned for faster iteration, especially if you like command-line-centered work. Gemini CLI offers a free-access path that may be attractive to some learners. Claude Desktop can be useful for longer, conversational sessions. And Codex CLI belongs in the broader multi-platform picture for people who prefer that toolchain.

[JAMIE]
So the platform comparison is really about capability, comfort, and access.

[ALEX]
Yes. The chapter encourages choosing a primary platform, while also understanding that you may run the same agent across multiple platforms depending on the task.

[JAMIE]
Can you give an example?

[ALEX]
Sure. You might discover and discuss an issue in GitHub's web interface, investigate locally in VS Code, and then use a CLI-based workflow for fast iteration or scripting. Same conceptual agent, different interaction layer.

[JAMIE]
And the chapter includes learning paths by platform.

[ALEX]
It does. Path A is for people who use VS Code and is the recommended path for most learners. Path B is for people who prefer the command line. Path C is for learners who want the best of both.

[JAMIE]
There's also explicit accessibility guidance by platform, which I'm glad to see.

[ALEX]
Very important. The chapter addresses screen reader, low vision, and keyboard navigation considerations across platforms. That means learners should actively evaluate not just what a platform can do, but how accessible it is for them in practice.

[JAMIE]
So "best platform" is personal, not universal.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Next steps in this section are: choose your primary platform, run a simple agent there, and compare whether another platform gives you a better accessible experience.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now for the hands-on reference section. This is where specific agents are introduced.

[ALEX]
Yes, and the chapter first distinguishes two types of agents: informational agents and task-oriented agents.

[JAMIE]
Informational means read-only, analysis, summaries, status reports.

[ALEX]
Right. Task-oriented means agents that may edit files, run commands, or take more direct action, depending on the platform and permissions.

[JAMIE]
Let's go one by one through the featured examples.

[ALEX]
Agent one is daily briefing. Its job is to produce a morning overview of what needs your attention.

[JAMIE]
What kinds of things show up in that briefing?

[ALEX]
The chapter gives a structured output format that may include issues opened in the last twenty-four hours, pull requests awaiting your review, CI failures on your branches, security alerts, and community activity.

[JAMIE]
So it's a prioritization assistant.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Example commands are short, like asking for a morning briefing. The output is organized so you can scan it quickly.

[JAMIE]
Agent two is issue tracker.

[ALEX]
That agent helps with issue management. It can find open issues, especially by label or other criteria, and support triage thinking.

[JAMIE]
The example output includes open issues labeled good-first-issue, broken into high and medium priority, plus a drafted reply for a particular issue.

[ALEX]
Yes, and that's a good teaching moment: a drafted reply is not a final reply. It's a starting point that you must judge, revise, and own.

[JAMIE]
Agent three is pull request review.

[ALEX]
A very useful one, if you already know how to review manually. Its output may include a summary, a risk assessment, what could break, high-impact areas, a change map for specific files, suggested inline comments, and a recommendation such as approve with minor changes.

[JAMIE]
That sounds impressive"”and dangerous if someone trusts it blindly.

[ALEX]
Exactly. A confident review summary can be wrong. The agent is useful because it helps you notice patterns and focus your attention. It does not replace your responsibility to read the diff and understand the impact.

[JAMIE]
Agent four is analytics.

[ALEX]
Right. Team analytics looks at contribution summaries, active contributors, high-churn files, review turnaround time, and trends. This can help maintainers understand workflow patterns, but again, interpretation matters.

[JAMIE]
Agent five is insiders accessibility tracker.

[ALEX]
That one monitors accessibility-related changes. The example output includes recent accessibility changes, issues found, specific problems like a heading hierarchy skip or non-descriptive link text, positive changes such as an added ARIA label, and recommendations.

[JAMIE]
I noticed the example even references a VS Code setup heading inside that output.

[ALEX]
Yes, which reinforces that these agents can point at concrete artifacts in docs or code. But you still verify the underlying file and context yourself.

[JAMIE]
And agent six is template builder.

[ALEX]
An interactive issue template wizard. Instead of asking you to manually remember every field type and YAML detail, it can guide template creation. But once again, it's most useful if you have already built and tested templates manually, because then you can tell whether the generated structure actually fits your project.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Then there's a section on slash commands and prompts. Why isolate that as its own topic?

[ALEX]
Because prompt ergonomics matter. A good agent can still be hard to use if you don't understand how to invoke it effectively. The chapter highlights the most useful slash commands for the workshop and gives a quick reference.

[JAMIE]
And it teaches how to read slash command definitions, not just memorize command names.

[ALEX]
Yes. That's crucial. If you read a slash command definition carefully, you can usually infer the intended behavior, scope, and output style. The example slash command in the chapter is an accessibility update command, and the important question is not merely "what do I type," but "what behavior should I expect when I type it?"

[JAMIE]
So the learning cards here would be: read the definition, understand the behavior, use short targeted prompts, and verify the output.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now my favorite part: contributing to the ecosystem.

[ALEX]
This chapter is very strong on that. It explains two types of custom agents and then shows the general file structure of an agent.

[JAMIE]
Let's list that structure in human terms.

[ALEX]
An agent definition typically includes its purpose, its capabilities, its domain knowledge, its responsibilities, and response guidelines. There's also frontmatter"”metadata that describes what kind of agent it is and how it should behave.

[JAMIE]
And the distinction between informational and task-oriented shows up again in the metadata.

[ALEX]
Right. Informational agents are read-only and limited to GitHub tools or similar lookup behavior. Task-oriented agents may edit files, execute shell commands, or use APIs, depending on environment permissions.

[JAMIE]
The chapter gives an informational example first.

[ALEX]
Yes, the insiders accessibility tracker. That shows a read-only monitoring pattern.

[JAMIE]
And then a task-oriented example: the Markdown Accessibility Assistant.

[ALEX]
Exactly. That example introduces a key pattern called tiered decision-making.

[JAMIE]
Meaning the agent doesn't immediately charge ahead with edits.

[ALEX]
Correct. It can reason in steps: assess, identify issues, suggest or preview changes, and only then act more directly when appropriate. That pattern is especially important for accessibility work, where blind or low-vision contributors need output that is explainable, structured, and reviewable.

[JAMIE]
The chapter also lists required prerequisites for that assistant.

[ALEX]
Yes. Again, you need the underlying accessibility and markdown knowledge first. Otherwise the automation can obscure the reasoning you should be learning.

[JAMIE]
How do you invoke custom agents?

[ALEX]
Several ways: from VS Code chat, from the VS Code Agents window, from GitHub dot com task mode, and from issue assignment flows. There's also environment setup guidance for cloud agents so they can operate in GitHub-hosted contexts.

[JAMIE]
And if someone wants to create their own?

[ALEX]
The chapter walks them toward that. Start with the template builder agent as an exercise. First generate a template with the agent. Then extend the agent for your own project. Then do iterative refinement: compare what the agent produced, identify gaps, adjust instructions, and test again.

[JAMIE]
That's a very open-source way to learn.

[ALEX]
It is. You're not just consuming AI output; you're shaping the tool.

[JAMIE]
There are also two pre-built workflows highlighted.

[ALEX]
Yes. A guided accessibility template workflow and a guided security vulnerability template workflow. Each shows an invocation pattern, a workflow sequence, and in the security case an output shape.

[JAMIE]
And the exercises ask learners to notice what they're adding and then continue refining.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The "what comes next" message is that custom agents are not static. You evolve them as project needs become clearer.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Then the chapter zooms out again to the bigger picture: teams, orchestration, and work beyond the editor.

[ALEX]
Yes. The three teams connect because real workflows connect. Accessibility work touches repository workflow. Repository workflow touches developer tooling. Orchestrator agents help coordinate across those boundaries.

[JAMIE]
So instead of one specialized agent doing everything, you may have multiple agents with narrower jobs that are composed together.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The chapter also calls out high-impact agents to try first and the slash commands that save the most time.

[JAMIE]
And it introduces scope at three levels.

[ALEX]
Right. Scope one is your editor: accessibility agents helping you locally while you work. Scope two is your repository: agent definitions traveling with forks and collaborators. Scope three is the cloud: GitHub-hosted agentic workflows that operate through issues, pull requests, task mode, or other cloud contexts.

[JAMIE]
That helps learners understand where the action is happening.

[ALEX]
Yes, and it leads into deeper examples like auto-triaging accessibility issues. That kind of workflow can be powerful, but only if maintainers have clear criteria and review habits.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
We also need to cover GitHub Desktop, GitHub CLI, and Copilot CLI.

[ALEX]
Definitely. GitHub Desktop appears as a simpler graphical path for repository operations. Then GitHub CLI, the gh tool, is covered with installation, authentication, and common commands.

[JAMIE]
Again, we won't recite every command in audio, but we should explain the role.

[ALEX]
Exactly. GitHub CLI lets you inspect and manipulate GitHub resources from the terminal: repositories, issues, pull requests, authentication, and more. Then GitHub Copilot CLI extends that experience with AI assistance in the shell.

[JAMIE]
And the example tasks are very concrete: explain a command, suggest a command, or write a shell script.

[ALEX]
Yes. Those examples show where Copilot CLI can reduce friction. If you know what you want but not the syntax, it can help. If you have a command and want it explained in accessible terms, it can help. If you need a short script scaffold, it can help.

[JAMIE]
But the same caution applies.

[ALEX]
Always. Never paste or run shell commands you do not understand, especially commands that modify files, history, permissions, or remote state.

[JAMIE]
The example session in the chapter likely exists to show that rhythm: ask, inspect, understand, then decide.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And the learning cards for this section would emphasize that GitHub Desktop, GitHub CLI, and Copilot CLI are complementary tools, not competing identities.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There's also a quick-reference keyboard shortcut section.

[ALEX]
Yes. For this audience, that matters a lot. The chapter includes accessibility-agents quick-reference shortcuts, including opening Copilot Chat and navigating key workflows. Since shortcuts vary by keymap and platform, learners should verify them in their own environment. The important practice is to know both the shortcut path and the Command Palette path.

[JAMIE]
That way if a shortcut conflicts or isn't memorable, you still have a reliable route.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's finish with troubleshooting, because agents never fail at convenient times.

[ALEX]
Very true. The chapter includes several common failure modes. First: "agent not found."

[JAMIE]
What should learners check?

[ALEX]
Check whether the agent definition exists in the expected repository location, whether the platform supports that style of custom agent, whether the repository is open in the correct context, and whether you may need to reload or rescan the environment.

[JAMIE]
Second: the agent produces incorrect output.

[ALEX]
Then treat it as an analysis artifact, not truth. Compare it against the underlying issue, PR, file, or repository state. Tighten the prompt. Check whether the agent instructions are too vague. And if the agent itself needs improvement, that can become a contribution.

[JAMIE]
Third: slash command doesn't work.

[ALEX]
Check whether the command is supported in your current tool, whether the syntax matches the definition, and whether the command belongs to a different platform or agent context than the one you're using.

[JAMIE]
So troubleshooting here is partly technical and partly conceptual.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Sometimes the fix is "reload the window." Sometimes the fix is "I misunderstood what this tool can do."

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we close, can we pull together the authoritative-source idea one more time?

[ALEX]
Yes. This chapter repeatedly points back to GitHub Docs, GitHub Changelog, GitHub Copilot docs, custom instructions support matrices, and documentation about custom agents. That matters because AI features move quickly. If a menu label changes, if a support matrix expands, if the Agents window behavior shifts, the official docs outrank any static lesson.

[JAMIE]
So the durable learning here is not memorizing one interface screenshot.

[ALEX]
Right. The durable learning is: understand skill first, agent second; know how agent files travel with repositories; choose a platform that works for your workflow and accessibility needs; validate outputs against manual knowledge; read agent instructions; and contribute improvements when you find gaps.

[JAMIE]
Let me see if I can summarize the learner mindset. Don't ask, "Which agent is coolest?" Ask, "Which agent matches a skill I already have?" Don't ask, "Can I trust the output?" Ask, "How do I verify the output?" And don't ask, "What if the agent is imperfect?" Ask, "Can I improve it?"

[ALEX]
That is exactly the mindset this chapter wants.

[JAMIE]
And for the workshop tasks: map three to five agents to skills you already have, run one and evaluate it, read one agent's instructions closely, optionally contribute a fix or propose a new agent, and don't skip the feedback submission.

[ALEX]
Perfect. Accessibility agents are most powerful when they stay in partnership with human judgment, human skill, and accessible contribution workflows.

[JAMIE]
Which is a very fitting note for this course.

[ALEX]
It is. We'll stop there.

## 55 AI Agents Across 3 Teams and 5 Platforms

> **Day 2, Block 3 Material**
>
> [Accessibility Agents](https://github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents) is a growing open source ecosystem: **80 AI-powered agents** organized into **three teams** (Accessibility, GitHub Workflow, and Developer Tools), running on **five platforms** (GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Claude Desktop, and Codex CLI). This chapter introduces the full landscape. Explore the agents that match your interests and workflows - there is no fixed subset you are required to use.
>
> **The agents are only useful if you have already done the work manually.** An agent that summarizes issues is useless to someone who has never read an issue. An agent that reviews a diff is useless to someone who has never read a diff. The agent does not teach you the skill - it multiplies a skill you already have.

## 1. The Principle: Skill First, Agent Second

Accessibility Agents is not a way to skip learning GitHub. It is a way to amplify skills you have already built through deliberate practice.

The ecosystem includes 55 agents across three specialized teams, running on five different AI platforms. That scale makes this principle critical: every agent automates a sequence of steps you should already know how to do manually. If you do not know those steps by hand, you cannot:

- Verify that the agent's output is correct
- Catch when the agent misses context that only you have
- Edit the agent's drafts into something worth posting under your name
- Know when the agent is confidently wrong

### Every agent has a manual prerequisite. If you have not done the corresponding skill by hand, the agent is not ready for you yet - and you are not ready for it

This applies across all three teams and all 55 agents:

- **GitHub Workflow agents** automate repository navigation, issue triage, PR review, and contribution analytics - skills you practiced on Day 1
- **Accessibility agents** automate WCAG auditing, contrast checking, keyboard navigation review, and document scanning - knowledge from your accessibility training and the standards in [Appendix C](appendix-m-accessibility-standards.md)
- **Developer Tools agents** automate accessible coding patterns for Python, wxPython, and desktop applications - skills from your development experience

Before running any agent, the facilitator asks the same question:

> *"What would you do if you had to do this step manually right now?"*

That question is not rhetorical. Answer it before running the agent. If you cannot answer it, learn the manual skill first.

> **Exploration prompt:** As you browse the [full agent ecosystem](#3-the-ecosystem-55-agents-3-teams-5-platforms), identify which agents match workflows you already do by hand. Those are your starting points. On Day 2, you will also have the opportunity to contribute improvements, new patterns, or entirely new agents back to the project.

### Hook-Based Enforcement (Claude Code)

On Claude Code, Accessibility Agents includes a hook system that enforces accessibility standards automatically:

1. **Proactive detection hook** - scans every file edit for accessibility regressions before they are committed
2. **Edit gate hook** - blocks commits that introduce WCAG violations until they are fixed
3. **Session marker hook** - tracks which accessibility checks have run during the current session

This means accessibility enforcement happens whether or not the developer remembers to ask for it. The hooks run as part of the Claude Code lifecycle, not as an afterthought.

## 4. Agents in Detail - Hands-On Reference

This section walks through several agents in depth so you can see how they work, what they produce, and how to evaluate their output. These examples use GitHub Workflow agents because they build directly on Day 1 skills - but the same patterns apply to every agent in the ecosystem. After working through these examples, explore agents from any team that match your interests.

Open any agent file in VS Code to read its full instructions: `.github/agents/[name].agent.md`

### Two Types of Agents

Before diving in, it helps to know that custom agents fall into two categories - this distinction affects what tool permissions they need and what they can do:

**Informational agents** search, analyze, and report. They respond in chat without modifying files. Examples: `@daily-briefing`, `@issue-tracker`, `@analytics`. These agents need only read and search tools (like `github/search_issues`, `github/issue_read`) - they are safer to trust with broad repository access and are simpler to build.

**Task-oriented agents** take action. They can read and edit files, run shell commands, create commits, and open pull requests. Examples: `@pr-review`, `@insiders-a11y-tracker`. These agents need a broader toolset (`read`, `edit`, `execute`, `github/*`) - and because they can make changes, their output always warrants human review before anything is posted or merged.

Many agents do both - they explain what they found (informational) and optionally make changes if you ask (task-oriented). The key question when you build your own is: *does this agent need to change files, or only to report?* Start informational. Expand to task-oriented only when the reporting alone is not enough.

## 6. Contributing to the Ecosystem

The 55 Accessibility Agents and 54+ slash commands are starting points. The `.agent.md` format is open - you can create your own agents for any repeatable workflow, and contribute them back to the project.

> **Think strategically about impact.** Before you build, ask: "Who benefits from this agent, and how often?" An agent that saves 100 people five minutes each week has more impact than an agent that saves one person an hour once. The best contributions solve problems that many people share.
>
> Source: [accessibility.github.com/documentation/guide/getting-started-with-agents/](https://accessibility.github.com/documentation/guide/getting-started-with-agents/)

### Two Types of Custom Agents

**Informational agents** - conversational; search, analyze, and present results:

- Perform GitHub searches with predefined scopes and filters
- Present results in specific structured formats
- Query GitHub API tools to answer questions

**Task-oriented agents** - active; edit files, run commands, submit PRs:

- Execute external tools (linters, test suites, axe-core)
- Make direct file edits based on findings
- Create pull requests with proposed changes
- Combine both: explain issues (informational) and fix them (task-oriented)

### Agent File Structure

> **See also:** [Appendix L: Agents Reference](appendix-l-agents-reference.md) has the complete agent.md format specification and examples.

Every `.agent.md` file has two parts: **YAML frontmatter** (metadata) and a **system prompt** (markdown body).

```markdown
name: agent-name
description: One-sentence description of what the agent does
tools:
  - github/search_issues
  - github/issue_read

## Purpose
Brief explanation of when to use this agent

## Your Capabilities
- What the agent can find or do

## Domain Knowledge
Specific query patterns, filters, or product knowledge

## Responsibilities
Step-by-step behavioral rules

## Response Guidelines
How to format output
```

### Frontmatter fields

| Field | Required | Description |
| -------  | ----------  | -------------  |
| `name` | Recommended | How the agent appears in the agent picker |
| `description` | Recommended | Shown in agent lists |
| `tools` | Optional | Restricts tool access; omit to grant all tools |

**Restricting tool access** is a security best practice - only grant what the agent actually needs:

```yaml
# Informational agent - read-only GitHub tools only
tools: ["github/search_issues", "github/issue_read"]

# Task-oriented agent - file editing, shell execution, and GitHub API
tools:
  - read
  - edit
  - search
  - execute
  - github/*
```

### Example: Informational Agent - `@insiders-a11y-tracker`

This agent monitors VS Code Insiders releases for accessibility improvements. It searches the `microsoft/vscode` repository using predefined GitHub query syntax, so you never have to remember the exact filter parameters.

#### Use it

1. Select `@insiders-a11y-tracker` from the agent picker
2. Ask: `what shipped this month?` or `any keyboard navigation improvements in January?`
3. The agent searches with `repo:microsoft/vscode is:closed milestone:"[Month] [Year]" label:accessibility label:insiders-released` and returns formatted results

**Prerequisite:** GitHub MCP server installed ([github.com/github/github-mcp-server](https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server))

### Example: Task-Oriented Agent - The Markdown Accessibility Assistant

The GitHub Accessibility team published a complete walkthrough for building a **Markdown Accessibility Assistant** - a task-oriented agent that reviews Markdown files for accessibility issues and makes direct fixes. It:

- Runs `markdownlint-cli2` to catch structural problems (heading skips, bare URLs, missing blank lines)
- Reviews link text for descriptiveness
- Flags missing or inadequate alt text and **waits for your approval** before changing it (alt text requires human judgment)
- Fixes heading hierarchy, list structure, and bare URL formatting directly
- Works both locally in VS Code (editing files) and on GitHub.com (reviewing PRs and committing fixes)

This agent is the automated version of the accessibility review skills you built during Day 1. The five principles it enforces are directly from GitHub's accessibility documentation.

**To build it:** Follow the step-by-step guide at [accessibility.github.com/documentation/guide/getting-started-with-agents](https://accessibility.github.com/documentation/guide/getting-started-with-agents/) - the YAML frontmatter, each section of the system prompt, and the complete agent file are all shown.

### Key Pattern: Tiered Decision-Making

From the guide:

```text
For objective issues (link text, heading hierarchy, list structure):
  → Agent makes the fix directly

For subjective issues (alt text, plain language):
  → Agent flags the issue, explains why it matters, suggests a fix,
    and waits for human approval before making changes
```

This tiered approach - automate what can be objectively evaluated, flag what needs human judgment - is the right model for any accessibility agent. It maximizes the agent's value while keeping humans in control of decisions that require context.

### Required Prerequisites for the Markdown Accessibility Assistant

- GitHub MCP server installed and configured ([github.com/github/github-mcp-server](https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server))
- Node.js installed (for `npx markdownlint-cli2`)

## 7. The Bigger Picture: Teams, Orchestration, and Beyond VS Code

The 55 agents are not 55 independent tools. They are organized into three teams that work together, and several orchestrator agents exist specifically to coordinate multi-agent workflows.

### How the Three Teams Connect

In practice, a single task often spans multiple teams:

- You ask `@daily-briefing` (GitHub Workflow) for your morning report. It flags a PR that changes ARIA attributes.
- You ask `@pr-review` (GitHub Workflow) to generate a structured review of that PR. The review notes potential accessibility impact.
- You invoke `@aria-specialist` (Accessibility) to deep-check the ARIA changes. It identifies a missing `aria-expanded` state on a disclosure widget.
- You fix the issue using patterns from `@desktop-a11y-specialist` (Developer Tools) if it is a desktop application, or directly in the HTML if it is a web project.

No single agent covers the entire workflow. The teams complement each other: GitHub Workflow agents surface *what happened*, Accessibility agents evaluate *whether it is correct*, and Developer Tools agents help you *implement the fix*.

The same Markdown-authored pattern extends further:

- **Reaches:** Every repository your GitHub account has access to
- **Scale:** All 55 agents available when the workspace is open

- **File lives in:** `.github/agents/[name].agent.md` in the repo
- **Triggered by:** Any contributor who has Copilot and opens the repo as a VS Code workspace
- **Runs on:** Their machine, using their Copilot subscription
- **Reaches:** Their GitHub account's repositories

### Scope 3: The Cloud (GitHub Agentic Workflows)

- **File lives in:** `.github/workflows/[name].md` (same folder as standard Actions YAML)
- **Triggered by:** Any GitHub event - `issues: opened`, `pull_request: created`, `schedule:`
- **Runs on:** GitHub Actions infrastructure, serverlessly
- **Reaches:** The repository where the workflow is defined

No VS Code required. No local machine required. The workflow runs whether or not anyone is watching - when an issue is opened at 3am, the agentic response fires.

**The link between Accessibility Agents and Agentic Workflows:** Both use Markdown-authored instructions. Both define intent in plain language. Both travel with the repository. ### Learning Cards: GitHub Desktop, GitHub CLI, and Copilot CLI

**Screen reader users:**

- GitHub Desktop is a native application -- on Windows it uses UI Automation, not a browser DOM; your screen reader's object navigation (NVDA: `Insert+Numpad`) rather than browse mode is the correct approach for navigating its interface
- GitHub CLI (`gh`) is entirely terminal-based; all output is plain text that your screen reader reads line by line -- pipe verbose output through `| head -20` or `| Select-Object -First 20` to avoid overwhelming your speech buffer
- Copilot CLI (`gh copilot suggest` and `gh copilot explain`) presents interactive prompts in the terminal; listen for the "Run this command? (Y/n)" confirmation before pressing Enter to avoid executing unreviewed commands

**Low-vision users:**

- GitHub Desktop inherits your Windows display scaling -- if text appears small, increase system-level scaling (Settings > Display > Scale) rather than looking for an in-app zoom option
- Terminal output from `gh` and `gh copilot` uses your terminal's font and color settings; configure your terminal profile (Windows Terminal settings or iTerm2 preferences) with a high-contrast color scheme and large font for comfortable reading
- Copilot CLI suggestions appear as plain text in the terminal, not in a styled panel -- they are easy to miss among other output; look for the indented suggestion block immediately after your prompt

**Sighted users:**

- GitHub Desktop provides a visual diff view, branch graph, and drag-and-drop staging that are unavailable in the CLI -- use Desktop when you want a spatial overview of complex changes
- GitHub CLI is scriptable; combine `gh issue list`, `gh pr list`, and `gh api` with shell pipelines to build custom dashboards without leaving the terminal
- Copilot CLI complements (not replaces) your Git knowledge -- use `gh copilot explain` when you encounter an unfamiliar Git command in documentation, and `gh copilot suggest` when you know what you want to do but not the exact syntax

## Troubleshooting

### "Agent not found"

**Issue:** Typing `@agent-name` shows "No agent found."

#### Solutions

1. Verify `.github/agents/[name].agent.md` exists in your workspace
2. Reload VS Code window: `Ctrl+Shift+P` → "Reload Window"
3. Check file naming: must end with `.agent.md`
4. Verify YAML frontmatter is valid (no syntax errors)

### Agent produces incorrect output

**Issue:** Agent's response is wrong or misses context.

#### Solutions

1. **Provide more context in your prompt:** Be specific about what you need
2. **Use @ mentions:** Reference specific files or selections (`@filename.md`, `#selection`)
3. **Check the agent's prerequisites:** Did you do the manual work first?
4. **Review the agent's instructions:** Open `.github/agents/[name].agent.md` and read what it's supposed to do

### Slash command doesn't work

**Issue:** `/command` shows "Command not found."

#### Solutions

1. Verify `.github/prompts/[name].md` exists
2. Reload window: `Ctrl+Shift+P` → "Reload Window"
3. Check file naming: must be a `.md` file in `.github/prompts/`
4. Try typing the full command name (autocomplete may be incomplete)

[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
